chapters.title: Chapter 1: The Two Ways Property Pays You

lessons.title: Total Return: Putting Yield and Appreciation on One Scale

children.text: Two property ads land on the same day in Ahmedabad. One shouts "6.4% rental yield, pre-leased shop in Satellite." The other says "South Bopal prices up 6% a year, book your 2BHK now." Both cost ₹75 lakh. The first ad shows only rent, the second shows only price growth, and neither tells you what you would actually earn. This lesson gives you the one number that does: total return. By the end, you will be able to put any flat, shop, REIT, FD or index fund on the same scale and see which one really pays more.

body.text: Rental yield and appreciation are only halves of the answer. Total return is the whole answer, and it is the only fair way to compare a flat with a shop, a REIT or a Nifty index fund.

markDefs.definition: The part of total return that comes from cash paid to you, such as rent, interest or dividends.
The part of total return that comes from a rise in the asset's price.

children.text: (appreciation), both measured against the price at the start of the year.

body.caption: The full formula for a single year.
The same thing, split into its two engines. For one year, the two versions give exactly the same answer.

children.text: Take the South Bopal flat. It rents for ₹18,000 a month, or ₹2.16 lakh a year, a gross yield of 2.88%. If its price rises 6% in the year, from ₹75 lakh to ₹79.5 lakh, the price gain is ₹4.5 lakh. Total return = (₹2.16 lakh + ₹4.5 lakh) ÷ ₹75 lakh × 100 = 8.88%. Split into engines: 2.88% yield + 6% appreciation = 8.88%. We use gross yield here to keep the arithmetic clean; Chapter 2 shows how to net off costs.

body.title: The two halves
body.textWithBlank: For a single year, total return = rental yield + ___.
body.explanation: Total return is the income engine (rental yield) plus the growth engine (appreciation), both measured against the starting price.

children.text: Flat vs Shop: Same Price, Different Engines

body.caption: Two ₹75 lakh properties in Ahmedabad, expected first-year return (illustrative)

body.title: South Bopal flat: where the 8.88% comes from
Satellite shop: where the 8.4% comes from

body.text: The totals are within half a percentage point of each other, but the risks are not. Most of the shop's return is written into a lease you can read today, so its big risk is losing the tenant. Most of the flat's return is a price forecast, so its big risk is the forecast being wrong. Same total, very different bet.

children.text: Over Ten Years, the Engines Compound Differently

One-year numbers hide something important. Appreciation compounds automatically: next year's 6% is earned on a bigger price. Rent does not compound on its own. It lands in your bank account, and it grows your wealth only if you reinvest it. Let us run both properties for ten years, assuming each property's rent grows at the same rate as its price and rent arrives at the end of each year.

body.title: Cumulative Gain on ₹75 Lakh, Rent Not Reinvested (₹ lakh)

children.text: If the rent is simply spent, the flat finishes ₹18.8 lakh ahead. If every rupee of rent goes into a debt fund or FD earning 7%, the gap shrinks to about ₹9.2 lakh. The shop depends far more on what you do with its cash. That is the hidden rule of high-yield property: its long-run return is only as good as your reinvestment discipline.

body.title: Show me the math: the ten-year numbers

content.caption: P = purchase price, g = annual growth, n = years. Flat: ₹75 lakh × 1.06^10 = ₹75 lakh × 1.7908 = ₹134.3 lakh.
R = first year's rent. Flat: ₹2.16 lakh × (1.7908 − 1) ÷ 0.06 = ₹2.16 lakh × 13.18 = ₹28.5 lakh.
i = reinvestment rate. Shop: ₹4.8 lakh × (1.9672 − 1.2190) ÷ 0.05 = ₹4.8 lakh × 14.96 = ₹71.8 lakh.

children.text: Shop value: ₹75 lakh × 1.02^10 = ₹75 lakh × 1.2190 = ₹91.4 lakh. Shop rent collected: ₹4.8 lakh × (1.2190 − 1) ÷ 0.02 = ₹52.6 lakh. Flat rent reinvested: ₹2.16 lakh × (1.9672 − 1.7908) ÷ 0.01 = ₹38.1 lakh. These formulas assume rent is received at the end of each year and grows at the same rate as the price.

body.title: Why the gap widens
body.question: In year one, the flat's expected total return (8.88%) is only slightly above the shop's (8.4%). Why does the flat pull well ahead by year ten when rent is not reinvested?
options: Appreciation compounds on a growing price, while rent that is spent does not compound
Flats always outperform shops over long periods
Rent from shops is taxed while rent from flats is not
Stamp duty is lower on flats than on shops
body.explanation: The flat's 6% growth is earned on a bigger base every year, and its rent grows at 6% too. The shop's return is mostly cash that leaves the asset. Unless that cash is reinvested, it adds up in a straight line instead of compounding. The other options are not true as general rules.

children.text: Property on the Same Scale as Everything Else
Every investment you can buy in India, from an SBI FD to a Nifty 50 index fund on Zerodha, has the same two engines. Only the mix changes. Seeing the mix tells you where the risk sits.

body.caption: Income engine vs growth engine across asset classes

cells: None: you get back the same rupees

body.title: Total return on a REIT
body.prompt: A REIT listed on NSE trades at ₹360 per unit. Over the year it distributes ₹24 per unit, and by year-end the unit price is ₹378. What was the one-year total return? Round to one decimal place.
body.explanation: Distribution yield = ₹24 ÷ ₹360 = 6.67%. Price appreciation = (₹378 − ₹360) ÷ ₹360 = 5%. Total return = (₹24 + ₹18) ÷ ₹360 × 100 = 11.67%, or about 11.7%. Exactly the same formula as a flat: income plus price change, divided by the starting value.

children.text: The Costs Standing Between You and Total Return

markDefs.definition: The reduction in return caused by one-time buying and selling costs such as stamp duty, registration and brokerage.

children.text: A REIT costs a few rupees in brokerage to buy and sell. A flat does not. Assume the South Bopal flat carries about 7% in buying costs (stamp duty, registration and brokerage, roughly ₹5.25 lakh) and 1% brokerage when you sell. This
is paid once, so it hurts short holding periods badly and long ones far less. Here is the flat's total gain after both costs, rent not reinvested and before tax.

body.text: Sell a flat within a year or two and buying and selling costs can wipe out almost the entire total return. Property's total return only becomes meaningful over long holding periods. If you might need the money within five years, a low-cost listed alternative such as a REIT is usually a better fit.

body.title: Same total, different goal
body.scenario: Dr. Fatima Rahman, a 54-year-old doctor in Kochi, has ₹1.5 crore to invest and plans to retire in six years, when a steady monthly income will matter most. Option A: a villa in Kakkanad, expected gross yield 1.8% and expected appreciation 7% a year. Option B: a pre-leased office unit near Infopark, Kakkanad, with a gross yield of 7% and expected appreciation of 2% a year.
body.prompt: Calculate the expected total return on each option. Then explain which option fits the goal better, and what else Dr. Rahman should consider.
body.modelAnswer:
1. Option A: 1.8% + 7% = 8.8% expected total return. Option B: 7% + 2% = 9% expected total return. On paper, they are almost identical.
2. The goal decides it. Dr. Rahman wants income at retirement. Option B delivers about ₹10.5 lakh a year in rent from day one (7% of ₹1.5 crore). Option A delivers about ₹2.7 lakh a year, and the rest of its return arrives only if the villa is sold.
3. Switching later is costly. Selling the villa in six years to buy an income asset means paying selling brokerage now and stamp duty, registration and brokerage again on the new purchase, which eats into the gain.
4. Option A's 7% is a forecast; Option B's 7% yield is a contract. But Option B's risk is real too: check the tenant's strength, the lease lock-in, the escalation clause and how long a vacancy near Infopark typically lasts.
5. Until retirement, Dr. Rahman should reinvest Option B's rent rather than spend it, since an income-heavy return compounds only if the cash is put back to work.
6. Tax matters: rent is taxed every year, while appreciation is taxed only on sale. Chapter 4 covers how that changes the comparison.

cards.definition: Income received plus the change in price, divided by the starting value.
The part of total return that comes from cash paid to you, such as rent, interest or dividends.
The part of total return that comes from a rise in the asset's price.
Putting income back to work so it compounds. Spent rent adds up in a straight line; reinvested rent compounds.
The hit to return from one-time buying and selling costs. It hurts short holding periods the most.
A REIT's annual payout per unit divided by its unit price: the REIT's version of rental yield.

points: Total return = (rent + change in price) ÷ starting value. For one year, it equals rental yield plus appreciation.
Two ₹75 lakh properties with total returns of 8.88% and 8.4% can carry completely different risks depending on which engine drives the return.
Appreciation compounds automatically on a growing price. Rent compounds only if you reinvest it.
High-yield property rewards reinvestment discipline; low-yield property rewards being right about price growth.
Every asset, from FDs and gold ETFs to Nifty index funds and REITs, can be broken into the same two engines.
One-time buying and selling costs crush short-term property returns, so total return only becomes meaningful over long holding periods.

body.text: This lesson is for education only and is not investment advice. The people, properties, prices, rents, growth rates and costs shown are illustrative assumptions, not forecasts. Stamp duty and registration charges vary by state, so verify current figures and consult a SEBI-registered investment adviser before making any decision.
